message.content: We're launching Fieldnote in six weeks and I need a campaign plan. It's a note-taking tool for people who work outdoors — surveyors, ecologists, site inspectors.

content.text: Before drafting anything I want to understand who we're actually talking to. Is the buyer the person in the field or someone above them?

message.content: Both, annoyingly. Individual surveyors buy it themselves, but the bigger money is consultancies buying 20 seats at a time.

content.text: Then this needs two tracks with different messages. For the individual the promise is that their notes survive the conditions — rain, gloves, no signal. For the consultancy the promise is that fieldwork arrives back at the office in a usable state instead of as photographs of a wet notebook.

message.content: The second one is the real pain. Half our early users came from a firm that lost a week of survey data.

content.text: That's the strongest thing we have and it should lead. I'll build the plan around loss of field data as the problem, not around note-taking as a category.

The brief now defines the problem as fieldwork that never makes it back intact, the audience as environmental and surveying consultancies of ten to fifty staff, and the proof as the offline-first sync model. Category framing is deliberately secondary.

message.content: What channels? We have almost no budget — maybe 8k total.

content.text: At 8,000 paid search is not viable against the established tools. I'd put nothing into paid acquisition and everything into three places where this audience already gathers: the professional institution newsletters, two industry conferences, and the regional practitioner forums.

For surveyors the chartered institution newsletter reaches roughly 12,000 practising members and sells a sponsored slot at about 1,400. For ecologists the equivalent body has a smaller list, near 4,000, at around 600. Both are read rather than filed, which is rarer than the numbers suggest.

message.content: Book both. What about the conferences?

content.text: There are two that matter in the window. The autumn surveying congress has a small-stand rate of 2,200 which is most of what's left, and a regional ecology forum at 350 for a speaking slot rather than a stand. The speaking slot is better value: this audience trusts a practitioner talking about their own fieldwork far more than a stand.

message.content: Agreed. Get someone who actually does the work to give the talk, not a marketer.

content.text: I'll approach the surveyor from the firm that lost the week of data — the story is theirs, it should be told by them. That leaves roughly 5,650 committed and 2,350 unallocated.

message.content: Now the email sequence. Five emails, and don't make them sound like marketing.

content.text: Drafted.

Five emails: the first is the lost-week story told plainly with no product mention; the second shows what offline capture actually does when there is no signal; the third is the office side, how notes arrive structured; the fourth is a working surveyor's fortnight with the tool; the fifth is a plain invitation to a trial. No urgency language, no discount, no exclamation marks.

message.content: Read the second one back to me.

content.text: It opens: 'A survey does not pause because the signal does. Fieldnote writes to the device first and syncs when there is something to sync to — the same notes, whether you are in a car park or three miles down a valley.' Then two short paragraphs on conflict handling when two people edit the same site record, and it closes on where the data sits.

message.content: That's decent. But cut the valley line, it sounds like an advert.

content.text: Cut. It now reads 'Fieldnote writes to the device first and syncs when there is something to sync to.' Plainer and it loses nothing.

message.content: Good. Now — I've been thinking. Lead with the consultancy angle everywhere, drop the individual track entirely. Simplify.

content.text: I'd push back on that. Roughly two thirds of our early users are individuals who then brought the tool into their firm — the individual track is how the consultancy deals start. Dropping it removes the path that produced the customers we have.

message.content: No, you're right, keep it. But make it clearly secondary — the consultancy story is what the money follows.

content.text: Restructured on that basis.

The consultancy narrative now leads every channel and owns the email sequence. The individual track survives as a self-serve trial path with its own short landing page, reached from the forums rather than pushed. It is present but it is not the headline.

message.content: What does the landing page need to say?

content.text: Very little. The problem in one line, a fifteen second capture-to-sync demonstration, the offline claim stated once with no qualifier, and a trial button. Anything else on that page competes with the demonstration, which is the only thing that convinces this audience.
I'll draft it and the surveyor reviews it for anything that rings false — that check matters more than a copy review, because this audience detects someone who has not done the work immediately.

message.content: How do we know if any of this worked? I don't want vanity numbers.

content.text: Three measures, none of them impressions. Trials started from each named source, so the newsletters and the talk can be told apart. Trial-to-team conversion, meaning an individual trial that becomes a multi-seat account, since that is the mechanism the plan depends on. And field retention: whether a trial user is still capturing notes in week three, because a note-taking tool that is abandoned by week three has not been adopted at all.

For a launch of this size: 300 trials across the six weeks, 8% of them converting to a team account, and 40% still capturing in week three. The first is a guess and should be treated as one. The other two are from the early-user cohort we already have, so they are grounded.

Three things. The surveyor has not agreed to give the talk yet, and the speaking slot and the whole story-led approach depend on it. The 2,350 of unallocated budget has no plan. And we have no answer for a consultancy that asks about data residency, which came up twice in early conversations and will come up again in a procurement discussion.

message.content: Data residency is a real gap. Note it as a blocker for the enterprise conversations, not for launch.

content.text: Recorded as a blocker on multi-seat procurement rather than on launch itself.

message.content: Where does the plan stand overall?

content.text: The brief, channel plan, five-email sequence, landing page copy and measurement plan are written. 5,650 of 8,000 is committed across two newsletters and one speaking slot. The consultancy narrative leads and the individual track is a secondary self-serve path. Open: the speaker has not confirmed, 2,350 is unallocated, and data residency is unanswered for procurement.
